notes.meaning: Paul tells Timothy how to correct people in the church with gentle respect. An older man should not be scolded harshly, but urged gently like one's own father. Younger men should be approached with brotherly kindness rather than looking down on them.

Timothy is told to treat older women with the honor given to a mother. He must treat younger women like sisters, keeping his thoughts, words, and actions completely pure. This family-like care protects both the minister and the church from scandal or temptation.

The church must give honor and real physical support to widows who are truly without help. In Bible times, honoring often meant providing money and daily food to those in need. The church family takes responsibility for women who have no relatives left to look after them.

If a widow has children or grandchildren, her care belongs to them first. Family members show their devotion to God by paying back the love and sacrifices their parents gave them growing up. Taking care of aged parents at home brings great pleasure to God.

A true widow in the biblical sense is a woman completely left alone with no relatives to help her. Because she has nowhere else to turn on earth, she places her complete hope in God. She spends her days and nights steadily praying, finding her strength and daily bread in the Lord.

A widow who chooses a self-indulgent life of luxury and bodily pleasure is spiritually dead, even though she is physically breathing. Living only for temporary thrills cuts a person off from the true life found in God. Such a person should not receive the support that belongs to needy, godly believers.

Timothy must teach these rules clearly to the congregation so that everyone knows their duty. When families support their elderly relatives and widows live holy lives, outsiders find no reason to criticize the church. Clear instruction keeps the whole community above reproach before the world.

Anyone who refuses to provide basic food and shelter for their own family members has denied what the Christian faith teaches. Even people who do not know God usually care for their own kin by natural affection. A believer who ignores needy relatives fails this basic duty and acts worse than an unbeliever.

Paul sets specific guidelines for a widow to be put on the church's official list of care and service. She must be at least sixty years old, an age when she is unlikely to remarry or find work. She must also have a record of faithful devotion to her husband during her married life.

To be enrolled, a widow must also be well known for a lifetime of good works. She should have raised children well, welcomed strangers into her home, and humbly served other believers, such as washing their feet. Her life must show that she gladly jumped in to help people in distress.

Younger widows should not be placed on this official church list. As time passes, their natural physical desires may awaken, leading them to want to marry again. If they have pledged themselves to lifelong church service, these new desires can pull them away from their commitment to Christ.

By turning back to marriage after making a pledge of dedicated service, younger widows would bring judgment on themselves. They would be guilty of breaking their first promise of devoted service made to Christ and his church. Paul warns against making solemn commitments that young people cannot easily keep.

Without family duties or active work, younger widows on church support easily fall into bad habits of idleness. They risk wandering from house to house, gossiping and prying into affairs that are not their business. Paul warns that too much spare time can lead to spreading harmful talk.

Paul advises younger widows to remarry, bear children, and manage their own households. Filling their days with useful family duties protects them from idleness and bad habits. This path keeps them respectable and leaves enemies of the gospel with no excuse to speak evil of believers.

Paul points out that some younger widows had already wandered away from following Christ to follow Satan. They had fallen into idleness, worldly pleasures, or false teachings that wrecked their walk with God. This painful reality showed why strict rules were needed for the church list.

Any believing woman who has widowed relatives under her care must support them herself. Taking care of family at home prevents the local church from being weighed down with extra expenses. This frees up church funds to care for truly destitute widows who have no one else.

Church leaders, or elders, who govern the church well deserve honor and generous financial support. Paul places special value on those who pour their energy into preaching God's word and teaching the congregation. Caring well for faithful pastors allows them to devote themselves fully to their calling.

differ.view: This passage distinguishes between two kinds of church elders: ruling elders who help govern and teaching elders who preach and teach.
All elders share the one office of pastor or overseer and must be able to teach, though some may give more time and labor to public preaching.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic translations render elder here as priest, referring to the ordained priesthood that rules and teaches the faithful.

notes.meaning: Paul supports paying church workers by quoting two passages of Scripture. The first, from the law of Moses, forbids muzzling an ox so it can eat grain while working. The second, spoken by Jesus, states that any worker deserves fair pay for his labor.

Charges against a church elder should never be entertained based on mere gossip or a single person's complaint. A formal accusation requires the clear testimony of two or three credible witnesses. This protects leaders from malicious attacks while ensuring that real misconduct is handled through fair evidence.

When leaders persist in wrongdoing and are proven guilty, they must be publicly rebuked before the congregation. Open correction shows that the church takes sin seriously and plays no favorites. Seeing a public rebuke also instills a healthy fear of sin in everyone else.

Paul places Timothy under a solemn charge before God, Jesus Christ, and the holy angels who watch over the church. He must carry out these rules of church discipline fairly, without jumping to conclusions beforehand. No leader should receive special favors, and no accused person should be treated unfairly.

Timothy is warned not to rush into ordaining someone to church leadership by laying hands on them too quickly. If a church leader carelessly appoints an unfit person, he shares responsibility for the harm and sins that follow. Timothy must keep his own life and ministry pure from compromise.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Laying on hands here may refer to restoring disciplined, repentant sinners back into church fellowship rather than ordaining ministers.

notes.meaning: Paul pauses to give Timothy personal medical advice, telling him to stop drinking water only and take a little wine. Water in the ancient world was often poor, and Timothy suffered from frequent stomach trouble and sickness. Good health practices and moderate remedies are part of honoring God with one's body.

differ.view: Paul permits wine here solely as a medicinal remedy for sickness, not as an ordinary drink for Christians.
Scripture allows the moderate drinking of wine as a beverage, while condemning drunkenness.

notes.meaning: The sins of some people are plain to everyone, making their guilt clear even before any formal investigation. Other people hide their wrongful deeds, and their true character comes to light only later upon careful inquiry or at God's judgment. For this reason, leaders must not judge people too hastily.

In the same way, the good works of many believers are clear and obvious for all to see. Even when good deeds are done quietly in secret, they cannot stay hidden forever. God eventually brings both faithful service and secret faults into the open.
